\section{The decision, the forecast and the testimony}
\label{sec:lttv-forecast}

In March 2015 the CRTC told television distributors to offer, by March 2016, an entry-level service \enquote{priced at no more than \$25 (not including equipment) per month} \citep[para.~26]{crtc2015worldofchoice}. Every discretionary channel was to be available on its own or in small packages by March 2016, and in both forms by December 2016 \citep[para.~47]{crtc2015worldofchoice}. The policy came out of the \textit{Let's Talk TV} proceeding, at which, by one later account, \enquote{virtually all parties expressed concerns about potential impacts of unbundling} \citep[para.~xxii, p.~5]{nordicity2015television}.

In a report dated December 2015, and released by its authors' later account in January 2016 \citep{miller2022rights}, Nordicity and Peter Miller published \textit{Canadian Television 2020}. It was prepared for ACTRA, the Canadian Media Guild, the Directors Guild of Canada, Friends of Canadian Broadcasting and Unifor \citep{nordicity2015television}. It modelled two worlds from 2015 to 2020: a baseline with \enquote{technological and consumer behaviour changes, assuming that the pre-existing broadcasting regulatory regime remains}, and the same world with the CRTC's decisions overlaid \citep[para.~ii, p.~1]{nordicity2015television}. Every headline number is the gap between the two. A third scenario, with the decisions modified, isn't checked here.

By 2020, the report concluded, the decisions were \enquote{likely to result in a loss of 15,130 FTEs of employment in the Canadian economy}, counted in full-time equivalents, along with \$\lttvGDPTotal{} million of GDP. Of those jobs, \lttvJobsDirect{} were directly in broadcasting and production and \lttvJobsSpinoff{} in other sectors \citep[para.~xliv and Table~1, p.~12]{nordicity2015television}. Those figures sit at the end of a chain. Subscribers move to cheaper unbundled packages; distributors lose retail revenue and pass most of the loss to Canadian channels as lower wholesale fees; weaker channels close; spending on Canadian programming falls; and input-output multipliers turn the spending into jobs and GDP.

The report states the assumptions that drive each link. Subscribers taking the entry-level service with a few chosen channels make up \lttvByopSixteen{} of all subscribers in 2016, \lttvByopSeventeen{} in 2017 and \lttvByopEighteen{} from 2018 \citep[Table~18, p.~76]{nordicity2015television}. Distributors pass \enquote{75\% of their retail revenue loss to Canadian programming services}, having attributed \lttvReportCanShare{} of that loss to Canadian services \citep[paras.~206--207, p.~77]{nordicity2015television}. By 2020, \lttvReportClosuresVI{} of the large integrated companies' Category A and B channels close, and \lttvReportClosuresIndep{} of the independents' \citep[paras.~232--233, p.~85]{nordicity2015television}.

By 2020 the model takes \$\lttvSpecImpactTwenty{} million (\lttvSpecShareTwenty{}) a year out of specialty and pay channels' revenue and \$\lttvBDUImpactTwenty{} million (\lttvBDUShareTwenty{}) out of distributors' revenue, against the baseline \citep[paras.~xxvi--xxvii]{nordicity2015television}.

\subsection{What the committee heard}

On 12 April 2016 Ian Morrison of Friends of Canadian Broadcasting, accompanied by Miller, put the report to the Commons Standing Committee on Canadian Heritage. Its key findings, he said, were that \enquote{by 2020, some 15,130 media jobs will be lost}, along with \enquote{a \$400-million drop in Canadian program expenditures} that was \enquote{18\% of what now exists}, \enquote{all of this as the direct result of Let's Talk TV regulatory changes}. He added that the authors had \enquote{advanced proposals to reduce the negative impact of the CRTC's decisions by as much as 75\%} \citep[time marks 0900--0905]{commons2016chpc8}.

Two of these phrases depart from the report. The \lttvJobsTotal{} FTEs are economy-wide, and \lttvJobsSpinoff{} of them are spin-off employment in other sectors, so \enquote{media jobs} misdescribes them; and the report describes its \lttvCPEShareStated{} as a share of projected 2020 baseline spending, not of current spending. The \$400 million rounds the report's \$399 million, and \enquote{direct result} attributes the losses to the decisions, as the report does, though \enquote{will be lost} is firmer than the report's \enquote{likely}. The 18\% itself is the report's, and its own figures don't reproduce it. The report's own baseline-scenario figures put 2020 Canadian programming expenditure at \$\lttvCPEBaselineTwenty{} million, so its \$\lttvCPEImpactTwenty{} million reduction is \lttvCPEShareTwenty{} of baseline, not the \lttvCPEShareStated{} its text states \citep[para.~239; Figs.~8, 9, 43]{nordicity2015television}. Against the report's own forecast for 2015, the reduction is \lttvCPEShareFifteen{}, and against what existed when Morrison spoke, the CRTC's count of 2015 spending (\$\lttvCPECRTCFifteen{} million), it's \lttvCPEShareCRTCFifteen{} \citep{crtc2017sfs2016}. None of the \lttvCPENCandidates{} shares tested, built from the report's figures over \lttvCPENDenominators{} denominators and its two impact figures, gives \lttvCPEShareStated{} (table~\ref{tab:cpe-denominators}).

Responding to a question about the \$25 bundle, one month after the entry-level service launched, Morrison cited a much lower uptake figure than the report's: \enquote{the best estimates I've seen, Mr.~Waugh, are that about 4\% of Canadians will go for it} \citep[time marks 0920--0925]{commons2016chpc8}. He didn't say how it bore on the job estimate.

\section{How the forecast was checked}
\label{sec:lttv-method}

The prediction record (forecasters, quantities, paths by year, stated assumptions) was committed before any CRTC outcome series was downloaded. I then re-read the report's two paths from the data labels on its charts, checking every value against the totals in its text, and ran a design analysis by fake-data simulation before opening any CRTC outcome file \citep{gelman2014types, gelman2020workflow}. It asked, for each forecast quantity, whether the outcome could separate a world in which the report's impact occurred from one in which it didn't, given that the baseline itself could be wrong.

That last clause is the hard part. In retrospective analysis of regulation, \enquote{developing a credible counterfactual is the most demanding aspect}, and the baselines assumed beforehand \enquote{must be revisited} to see whether outside factors changed the result \citep[286]{morgenstern2018retrospective}. Here the counterfactual is the report's own no-reform baseline, itself a forecast of how television would have fared under streaming without the reforms. So the check treats the baseline's error as unknown, puts a range on it, and reports results across that range, much as \textcite{kane2026sffa} reports against more than one baseline.

It depended on the quantity. With the baseline's error set at the volatility of the report's own 2010--2014 data, specialty and pay revenue would be classified correctly in about \lttvDesignCorrectSpec{} of simulated worlds and distributors' revenue in about \lttvDesignCorrectBDU{}. Canadian programming expenditure, whose historical volatility was \lttvHistSDCPE{} a year, came out at \lttvDesignCorrectCPE{}, so it was set aside in advance as descriptive.

The outcome measure is a single number, \(k\): the observed shortfall below the report's baseline over 2016--2019, the four years before the pandemic, as a multiple of the report's own forecast impact, so that \(k=0\) is the report's no-reform path and \(k=1\) its forecast. In logs, \(\log B_t-\log Y_t=k\,\delta_t+e_t\), where \(B_t\) is the report's baseline, \(Y_t\) the outcome, \(\delta_t\) the report's forecast shortfall, and \(e_t\) the baseline's error (positive when the baseline overstates what would have happened without the decisions), modelled as a random walk from 2014. Because that error accumulates from year to year, the estimate rests on changes in the gap between outcome and baseline rather than on its level: specialty and pay revenue's \(k\) is positive although that revenue stayed above the baseline in every year, because its excess over the baseline shrank, the direction the forecast predicted. The report's paths and the CRTC series are both in nominal dollars, and since \(k\) compares them year by year, deflating both by the same price index leaves it unchanged.

The 95\% interval for \(k\) comes from generalized least squares under that model, and it reflects only the assumed error in the baseline, so its width depends on how large that error is taken to be. The scale of that error is calibrated from an outside comparison, described below, rather than estimated from four years of outcomes, and the CRTC's administrative totals are treated as measured without error (appendix~\ref{app:methods}; inputs in table~\ref{tab:inputs}). The interval treats that scale as known and doesn't carry the uncertainty in the scale itself. As an illustration, if the historical volatility were treated as an estimate from four independent, normal annual changes, an interval using the \(t\) distribution with three degrees of freedom would be about \lttvTThreeWiden{} wider, and the distributors' interval would then include zero; even that illustration doesn't carry the uncertainty of the actual calibration rule.

\(k\) compares the outcome with the report's two forecast paths; it isn't an estimate of the decisions' causal effect, which would need a better counterfactual than the report's own baseline. A band of \(k\) built from the estimates the report cites (uptake between \lttvCitedUptakeLow{} and \lttvCitedUptakeHigh{}, closures up to \lttvCitedClosuresMult{} times the assumed rate) counts as consistent with the forecast; the band is my construction from those estimates, not one the report published. An outcome below the forecast path was to be reported as the forecast exceeded, never as confirmed.

The outcome series alone can't identify how wrong the baseline was, so the plan fixed an external check: the forecast of US Netflix subscribers that the report used for its US comparison (from Trefis), assumed unaffected by Canadian regulation, against Netflix's reported US paid memberships \citep{netflix2019form10k}. The report forecast \lttvNetflixFcEighteen{} million for 2018 and Netflix reported \lttvNetflixObsEighteen{} million, which by the pre-stated rule puts the error at \lttvSigmaTech{} a year, below the historical volatility of both revenue series. The CRTC series reproduce the report's 2012--2014 values within \lttvSpliceTol{} \citep{crtc2017sfs2016, crtc2021sfs2020}.

\section{What happened}
\label{sec:lttv-results}

Figure~\ref{fig:paths} shows each revenue series against the report's two paths. Specialty and pay revenue stayed above the report's no-reform baseline, by between \lttvSpecVsBaselineMin{} and \lttvSpecVsBaselineMax{} from 2016 to 2019, and ran between \lttvSpecVsLTTVMin{} and \lttvSpecVsLTTVMax{} \lttvSpecAboveLTTV{} the forecast path. Taken alone, the revenue \lttvSpecRevNomDir{} \lttvSpecRevNomChange{} in nominal dollars from 2015 to 2019 and \lttvSpecRevRealChange{} after inflation, while the report's baseline was flat in nominal dollars over 2016--2019 (table~\ref{tab:inputs}).

\begin{figure}[tbp]
\centering
\includegraphics[width=\textwidth]{figures/lttv_paths.pdf}
\caption{Revenue relative to the report's no-reform baseline, 2012--2019, in per cent of the baseline. The forecast path and the baseline are the report's (Figs.~41, 42); the partial recalculation holds uptake at the CRTC's June 2016 count and the exemption-order and closure dollar components fixed (post hoc); the outcome is the CRTC series (2016 edition to 2015, 2020 edition after; channels exclude exempt services). The shaded range is the pointwise 95\% range of the no-reform outcome under the baseline-error model at the pre-stated \(\sigma\) (\lttvSigmaReadSpec{} and \lttvSigmaReadBDU{} a year). Before 2015 the baseline is the report's own actual values. Both panels share one scale.}
\label{fig:paths}
\end{figure}

At the pre-stated calibration \(\hat k=\lttvKSpec\), with a standard error of \lttvKSpecSE{}. That's \lttvKSpecSEsFromZero{} standard errors from the no-reform path and \lttvKSpecSEsFromOne{} from the forecast, and the lowest value of the band built from the report's cited estimates, \lttvBandSpecLo{}, is \lttvKSpecSEsFromBandLo{} standard errors away. The pre-stated reading follows: the 95\% interval, \lttvKSpecLoTwo{} to \lttvKSpecHiTwo{}, lies below the band of \lttvBandSpecLo{} to \lttvBandSpecHi{}, so the outcome is inconsistent with the forecast at the report's assumed uptake.

That band assumes uptake between \lttvCitedUptakeLow{} and \lttvCitedUptakeHigh{}. The CRTC's count in June 2016 was far lower, and a 2017 survey, outside the plan's accepted sources, put uptake near the low end (section~\ref{sec:lttv-links}). Model-implied scenarios, an exploratory comparison, show how the projected \(k\) changes with the uptake assumption (table~\ref{tab:scenarios}). Recalculating the report's chain with uptake held at the CRTC's June 2016 count, \lttvUptakeJuneShare{}, and the exemption-order and closure components fixed, gives \(k=\lttvKPredSpecObsUptake\), \lttvKPredSpecObsUptakeSEs{} standard errors from the estimate. On the survey path, the CRTC's count in 2016 and 10\% from 2017, it gives \lttvKPredSpecSurvey{}, \lttvKPredSpecSurveySEs{} standard errors above it. Held at the \lttvMorrisonUptake{} Morrison cited it gives \lttvKPredSpecMorrison{} (\lttvKPredSpecMorrisonSEs{} standard errors away), and at the low end of the cited range \lttvKPredSpecCitedLow{} (\lttvKPredSpecCitedLowSEs{}). Since later uptake is unknown, two rising paths start from the 2016 count: rising to \lttvMorrisonUptake{} by 2019 gives \lttvKPredSpecRiseMorrison{} (\lttvKPredSpecRiseMorrisonSEs{}), and rising to \lttvCitedUptakeLow{} gives \lttvKPredSpecRiseCitedLow{} (\lttvKPredSpecRiseCitedLowSEs{}).

The scenarios don't fall to zero because the recalculation holds two components fixed: closures, and the exemption order for broadcasters' streaming services, which the report expected to \enquote{materially increase cord cutting and cord shaving} \citep[para.~xxiii]{nordicity2015television}. The report values both partly from the other components \citep[paras.~220, 234]{nordicity2015television}, so holding them fixed is my approximation, not a rerun of its model. At counted uptake the outcome is consistent with the scenario, which doesn't confirm the model. The fixed and rising uptake paths and the survey path were added after the outcome data was opened, the first two after an outside reader asked how a failed assumption can be told from a failed mechanism, and they sit beside the pre-stated reading rather than replacing it (table~\ref{tab:chronology}).

Distributors' revenue ran between \lttvBDUVsLTTVMin{} and \lttvBDUVsLTTVMax{} \lttvBDUAboveLTTV{} the report's forecast path, falling from \$\lttvBDURevFifteen{} million in 2015 to \$\lttvBDURevNineteen{} million in 2019, a fall of \lttvBDURevNomChange{}, or \lttvBDURevRealChange{} after inflation. Here \(\hat k=\lttvKBDU\) (standard error \lttvKBDUSE{}), \lttvKBDUSEsFromZero{} standard errors from the no-reform path and \lttvKBDUSEsFromOne{} from the forecast, so the outcome is consistent with the forecast and with the band of \lttvBandBDULo{} to \lttvBandBDUHi{} implied by the forecasters' inputs (interval \lttvKBDULoTwo{} to \lttvKBDUHiTwo{}). At the uptake the CRTC counted, the report's chain gives \(k=\lttvKPredBDUObsUptake\), \lttvKPredBDUObsUptakeSEs{} standard errors below the estimate at the pre-stated calibration but fewer than two with the 2017 or pooled calibration, the rescaled series or the offset model (\lttvBDUGapSEsSeventeen{}, \lttvBDUGapSEsPooled{}, \lttvBDUGapSEsRescaled{} and \lttvBDUGapSEsOffset{}); on the survey path it gives \lttvKPredBDUSurvey{}, \lttvKPredBDUSurveySEs{} standard errors below the estimate. That comparison doesn't by itself show where the shortfall came from.

Splitting the revenue separates the subscriber and per-subscriber contributions. Distributors' revenue is subscribers times revenue per subscriber, and the report's channels act on different factors: unbundling lowers revenue per subscriber and leaves subscriber numbers alone, while the exemption order adds cord cutting, 1.9\% of subscribers a year against 1.5\% in the baseline \citep[paras.~204--205, 216, 220; Tables~5, 21]{nordicity2015television}. Rebuilding the report's exemption-order component from its stated cord cutting and cord shaving reproduces it to within about \lttvDecCheckMaxDev{} in every year, so the scenario's split can be recovered (table~\ref{tab:decomposition}). The comparison is of changes from 2014, since in the report's actual years the CRTC's subscriber counts sit \lttvDecSubAlignLo{} to \lttvDecSubAlignHi{} below the report's and its revenue per subscriber \lttvDecPerAlignLo{} to \lttvDecPerAlignHi{} above. The comparison assumes the two series stay comparable after 2014: the report's subscriber series includes \enquote{non-reporting BDUs} (Fig.~17; BDUs, broadcasting distribution undertakings, is the CRTC's term for distributors), the CRTC's cover broadcast years ending 31 August, and revenue per subscriber here is total distributor revenue, which is broader than a package price.

By 2019, measured this way, subscribers had fallen a further \lttvDecSubObs{} below the report's baseline path, against \lttvDecSubFc{} in its scenario. Revenue per subscriber was \lttvDecPerObs{} below the baseline path, against \lttvDecPerFc{} in the scenario: it rose only \lttvRevPerSubObsGrowth{} in nominal dollars, from \$\lttvRevPerSubFourteen{} a month in 2014 to \$\lttvRevPerSubNineteen{} in 2019 (\lttvRevPerSubRealFall{} lower after inflation), while the baseline path rose \lttvRevPerSubBaseGrowth{}; its underlying price assumption was inflation plus one point, before an allowance for cord shaving \citep[Table~11, paras.~151--152]{nordicity2015television}. With uptake held at the June 2016 count and the other dollar components fixed, as in table~\ref{tab:scenarios}, the report's chain gives a per-subscriber shortfall of \lttvDecPerCounted{}, and on the survey path \lttvDecPerSurvey{}; so of the total revenue shortfall, in logs and measured from 2014, \lttvDecBeyondCounted{} lies beyond the chain at the CRTC's count and \lttvDecBeyondSurvey{} on the survey path. In nominal terms distributors' revenue fell \lttvBDURevFallFourteenNineteen{} from 2014 to 2019, as subscribers fell \lttvSubsFallFourteenNineteen{} and revenue per subscriber rose \lttvRevPerSubObsGrowth{}; against the report's rising baseline, about \lttvDecPerShare{} of the shortfall, measured in logs, is missing growth in revenue per subscriber.

The split was added after the outcome data was opened, under a rule fixed before it was computed (table~\ref{tab:chronology}); the counted-uptake comparison goes beyond that rule. It's an accounting identity, and revenue per subscriber is computed from the same totals, so the split locates the shortfall without observing prices or identifying causes. Subscriber losses exceed those in both of the report's paths compared here, and stagnant revenue per subscriber could reflect pricing, cord shaving to smaller packages, or the reforms themselves.

\begin{figure}[tbp]
\centering
\includegraphics[width=\textwidth]{figures/lttv_k_sigma.pdf}
\caption{The estimate of \(k\) and its 95\% interval as a function of the assumed annual error in the report's baseline, \(\sigma\). The solid vertical line marks the pre-stated calibration; dotted lines mark the values of \(\sigma\) used by the other calibrations (table~\ref{tab:calibrations}). The grey band is the range of \(k\) implied by the forecasters' cited inputs. The horizontal axis spans the plan's sensitivity range, 1\% to 8\% a year; intervals are conditional on \(\sigma\). The standard error is proportional to \(\sigma\), so the interval widens linearly while the estimate stays put.}
\label{fig:k-sigma}
\end{figure}

Both intervals depend on how wrong the baseline is taken to be (figure~\ref{fig:k-sigma}). The estimates don't move as the assumed error grows; the intervals widen in proportion. The specialty and pay interval reaches the band implied by the forecasters' inputs when the error reaches about \lttvCutoffSpec{} a year, and at the widest calibration, \lttvSigmaWidest{}, its upper end is \lttvKSpecHiWidest{}. The distributors' interval includes zero from about \lttvCutoffBDU{}. At the plan's upper value of 8\% a year, the specialty and pay interval, \lttvKSpecLoEight{} to \lttvKSpecHiEight{}, includes the forecast. None of the reported specialty and pay intervals excludes zero. The verdict labels in table~\ref{tab:calibrations} change as the assumed error crosses these values, though the estimate is the same throughout, and these label changes reflect the assumed error scale, not changes in the estimate \citep{gelmanStern2006difference}. Several calibrations were added after the outcome data was opened, so all of them are shown rather than the one that reads best \citep{gelman2014statcrisis}.

The pre-stated Netflix comparison puts the error at \lttvSigmaTech{} a year, below both series' historical volatility, so the historical volatility sets the pre-stated interval. Other defensible readings of the comparison give more: the 2016 miss gives \lttvSigmaTechSixteen{} a year and a pooled estimate \lttvSigmaTechPooled{}. Part of the 2016 miss is an inherited offset, since the report's 2015 starting figure (\lttvNetflixFcFifteen{} million) was already above Netflix's count (\lttvNetflixObsFifteen{} million) \citep{netflix2018form10k}. Measured as growth, Netflix's memberships outran the Trefis forecast the report used, by \lttvNetflixObsGrowth{} against \lttvNetflixFcGrowth{} from 2015 to 2018, which puts the error at \lttvSigmaGrowthEighteen{} a year.

A check of the model, added after the outcome data was opened, finds the specialty and pay residual concentrated in its first step. After fitting \(k\), the standardized changes in the baseline's error between observations are correlated and have variances below one. Divided by their standard deviations under the fit, the specialty and pay step from 2014 to 2016 is \lttvInnovSpecFirst{}, and the largest of the three later steps is \lttvInnovSpecLaterMax{} in absolute value; the distributors' steps show no such pattern. A one-time gap between the report's baseline and the CRTC series would produce this, though with four points so would a random walk whose later steps happened to be small.

Part of the specialty and pay gap is already visible in 2015, a year with no forecast impact, in the report's own figure for that year (itself a forecast). The CRTC later counted \$\lttvCRTCFifteenSpec{} million, \lttvGapFifteenSpec{} \lttvGapFifteenSpecDir{} the report's \$\lttvReportFifteenSpec{} million, against \lttvGapFourteenSpec{} in 2014 and negligible differences in 2012 and 2013, when the report's figures were actuals. Distributors' revenue shows no such change: the CRTC's counts run between \lttvGapRangeLoBDU{} and \lttvGapRangeHiBDU{} \lttvGapFifteenBDUDir{} the report's figures in every year from 2012 to 2015, a standing difference between the two series, with no new divergence in 2015. The 2016 and 2020 editions of the CRTC's summaries differ on 2016 by \lttvReleaseGapSpec{} for channels and \lttvReleaseGapBDU{} for distributors, so revisions between editions can't account for the gap. Allowing a level offset in the model, which absorbs both, gives \(\hat k=\lttvKSpecOffset\) (standard error \lttvKSpecOffsetSE{}) for specialty and pay revenue and \lttvKBDUOffset{} (\lttvKBDUOffsetSE{}) for distributors' revenue, leaving both pre-stated readings as they were; the distributors' counted-uptake comparison falls to \lttvBDUGapSEsOffset{} standard errors.

\section{The links in the chain}
\label{sec:lttv-links}

The report's numerical inputs can be compared with observed quantities without estimating a causal effect. The input on which most of the forecast depends is uptake. The report took its \lttvByopEighteen{} from outside estimates, the highest being Oliver Wyman's finding that \enquote{as many as 35\% of subscribers would be willing to switch to a skinny-basic/BYOP option} \citep[para.~201, p.~75]{nordicity2015television}, BYOP being the report's \enquote{Build Your Own Package} \citep[para.~202]{nordicity2015television}. The CRTC counted more than \lttvUptakeAprilN{} subscribers to the entry-level package five weeks after launch \citep{crtc2016basicpackage} and \lttvUptakeJuneN{} by 30 June 2016 \citep[para.~12]{crtc2016hearing0907}, about \lttvUptakeAprilShare{} and \lttvUptakeJuneShare{} of the 2016 subscriber total, against the report's \lttvByopSixteen{} for 2016. I found no later CRTC count. A survey by the Media Technology Monitor, released in August 2017, put adoption of starter packages at \enquote{just over 1 in 10 TV subscribers} and reported that 29\% of subscribers were adding individual channels or bundles to their packages \citep{mtm2017starter}. Surveys aren't among the sources the analysis plan accepted for uptake, and this one is self-reported and may not match the report's measure, the entry-level package with chosen channels; it's reported beside the planned reading, with the results under both. The release gives no fieldwork dates, sample size or margin of error; the survey path takes its \enquote{just over 1 in 10} as 10\%, a floor, and holds it through 2019, which is an assumption. Low uptake in 2016 may partly reflect how the package was sold, a possibility the report itself raised, that distributors might offer unbundling in a way \enquote{relatively unattractive from a price-value equation, so that very few Canadians opt for it} \citep[para.~78, n.~40, p.~34]{nordicity2015television}. The CRTC's hearing of September 2016 examined \enquote{the practices certain providers have adopted in offering} it \citep[para.~5]{crtc2016hearing0907}. Either way, uptake in mid-2016 was far below the level on which most of the forecast rested; whether it stayed there is the question the survey reopens.

The report also assumed a path for what distributors pay Canadian channels. In its no-reform baseline the monthly fee per subscriber for Canadian specialty and pay services rises \lttvBaseFeeGrowth{} from 2015 to 2019 \citep[Table~14, p.~67]{nordicity2015television}, and under the decisions it falls below that path as distributors pass on \lttvReportPassThrough{} of the retail loss attributed to Canadian services. What distributors paid Canadian channels rose from \$\lttvPayCanFifteen{} million in 2015 to \$\lttvPayCanNineteen{} million in 2019 while subscribers fell, so per subscriber it rose \lttvPerSubGrowth{}, and the Canadian share of all affiliation payments stayed near \lttvPayShareFifteen{} \citep[Table~U-T11]{crtc2019cmrbdu}. After inflation the total \lttvPayCanRealDir{} \lttvPayCanRealChange{} and the payment per subscriber \lttvPerSubRealDir{} \lttvPerSubRealChange{}; the comparison with the report's fee path needs no such adjustment, since that path is nominal too. The two fee measures differ by definition, so their growth is compared, not their levels. At uptake near the CRTC's count there would have been little loss to pass on, and the comparison would mainly show that payments grew faster than the report's baseline assumed; at the survey's level, the chain has fees falling relative to the baseline path, and observed payments instead grew faster than it. The aggregates can't say what fees would have been without the decisions.

The aggregates don't show why fees rose. Some of the payments stay inside the integrated groups, and the report itself expected the exemption order's impact on those groups to be partly offset by their streaming and broadband revenue \citep[para.~227, p.~83]{nordicity2015television}. The CRTC's wholesale code, scheduled to take effect in January 2016 \citep[p.~73, n.~82]{nordicity2015television}, is in both of the report's scenarios \citep[p.~72, n.~80]{nordicity2015television}, so its fee path already allows for it.

For the integrated companies, closures came out close to the report: between \lttvClosVILo{} and \lttvClosVIHi{} of their Category A and B channels stopped operating by 2019--2020, against the report's \lttvReportClosuresVI. For the independents the bounds, \lttvClosIndLo{} to \lttvClosIndHi{}, contain the report's \lttvReportClosuresIndep{} but are too wide to test it, because channels that left licensing for exemption can't be told apart from channels that closed. Both ranges classify Corus, which owns the former Shaw Media channels in the 2016 data, as independent; counted as integrated, as the analysis plan also required, it gives \lttvClosVICorusLo{} to \lttvClosVICorusHi{} for the integrated companies and \lttvClosIndCorusLo{} to \lttvClosIndCorusHi{} for the independents. Canadian programming expenditure, read only descriptively, stayed at or above the baseline path through 2019.

For two sectors, the CRTC's staff counts allow a descriptive comparison with the last link, from revenue to jobs \citep{crtc2017sfs2016, crtc2021sfs2020}. The report gives its direct FTE losses by sector against a baseline whose employment path it doesn't publish, so the comparison is with the change from 2015 and with the 2012--2015 trend carried forward, a crude stand-in for that baseline. Channels' staff fell from \lttvStaffChanFifteen{} in 2015 to \lttvStaffChanNineteen{} in 2019, \lttvStaffChanVsTrend{} \lttvStaffChanVsTrendDir{} the trend, against a forecast direct loss of \lttvStaffChanForecast{} by 2019. Distributors' staff stayed near its pre-2015 trend, \lttvStaffDistVsTrendEighteen{} \lttvStaffDistVsTrendEighteenDir{} it in 2018 and \lttvStaffDistVsTrend{} \lttvStaffDistVsTrendDir{} it in 2019, against a forecast direct loss of \lttvStaffDistForecast{} by 2019 \citep[Table~22, p.~91]{nordicity2015television}. The 2019 figure is a one-year jump that reverses the next year, which may be a reporting discontinuity.

Staff counts and revenue don't move together as the chain implies in either sector: channels cut staff while their revenue stayed above the baseline, and distributors' staffing stayed near trend while their revenue fell (annual series in table~\ref{tab:staff}). It's a descriptive mismatch, not a test of the model's employment prediction. The counts aren't the report's modelled full-time equivalents, the distributor series changes from an FTE count to a staff count between editions (the two differ by \lttvStaffDistVintageGap{} in 2016), and a straight-line trend is a weak counterfactual. The direction of the mismatch holds with the distributors' 2018 figure in place of 2019.
